nameStory: This beetle earned its name from its round head and its notorious habit of boring into apple trees. Unlike some borers with flattened or elongated heads, this species has a distinctly rounded noggin that makes it easy to distinguish from its relatives.
description: The Round-headed Apple Tree Borer is a longhorn beetle that spends most of its life as a wood-boring larva inside apple and other fruit trees. Adult beetles are medium-sized with long antennae typical of their family. The larvae create tunnels in tree trunks and branches, which can seriously damage or kill young trees. This species is found throughout Canada and the United States, making it a familiar pest to orchard growers.

idTips.label: Round head shape
idTips.description: The head appears noticeably rounded when viewed from above, unlike the flattened or elongated heads of other wood borers

idTips.label: Long antennae
idTips.description: Antennae are about as long as the body, segmented, and held out to the sides like a longhorn beetle should

idTips.label: Boring holes
idTips.description: Look for perfectly round exit holes about pencil-width in apple tree trunks, often with sawdust-like frass around them

idTips.label: Tree damage pattern
idTips.description: Larvae create winding galleries under the bark that you can feel as soft, spongy areas when pressed gently

idTips.label: Host tree preference
idTips.description: Almost always found on apple, crabapple, or related fruit trees rather than forest trees

habitat: Look for this beetle in orchards, around cultivated apple trees, and near wild crabapples throughout New England. They prefer sunny locations where fruit trees grow, from backyard gardens to commercial orchards. You'll also find them around ornamental crabapples in suburban areas and parks.

seasonality.spring: Adult beetles begin emerging from trees in late spring, leaving behind round exit holes. This is when you're most likely to spot the actual beetles crawling on tree bark.
seasonality.summer: Adults are active and mating, laying eggs in bark crevices of host trees. Look for fresh sawdust around the base of apple trees as new larvae begin boring.
seasonality.fall: Larvae continue developing inside trees, creating the soft, spongy areas under bark. Exit holes from earlier in the year become more noticeable as leaves fall.
seasonality.winter: Larvae overwinter deep in the wood. Trees may show stress from extensive boring, with bark peeling or branches dying back.

funFact: These beetles can take up to three years to complete their development inside a tree, spending most of their lives as hidden larvae munching tunnels through the wood while you walk past the tree completely unaware of the busy construction project happening inside!
confusionNotes: The round exit holes might be confused with other wood borers, but apple tree borers create distinctly circular holes about the diameter of a pencil, while most other borers make oval or irregular holes. Memory trick: Round beetle, round holes in apple trees.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called an "apple tree" borer, this beetle will also attack other members of the rose family including pear, quince, and mountain ash. The name reflects their preference and pest status rather than an exclusive relationship with apples.
compareHints: Unlike its relative the Elm Borer which targets elm trees and has a more elongated head, the Round-headed Apple Tree Borer has that distinctly rounded head and sticks to fruit trees. Both are longhorn beetles, but their host preferences and head shapes make them easy to distinguish once you know what to look for.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its closest relative in the same genus, the round-headed apple tree borer, the elm borer is distinguished primarily by its host tree preference - elm borers stick exclusively to elm species while apple tree borers prefer fruit trees and related plants in the rose family.
